summary: Reviews the security threats to marking signalling messages as emergency calls and to mapping a caller's location to the URI of the right Public Safety Answering Point. From these threats it derives security requirements for such systems. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When someone calls for help, the system must route them to the right emergency center. This lists the ways a trickster could mess that up and what must be protected.

questions: how are emergency calls routed to a psap securely
what security requirements apply to emergency call mapping
subtitle: The ways attackers could abuse emergency call marking and the mapping of a caller's location to a PSAP, and what the mapping protocol must do about them.

tldr.problem: Internet emergency calling relies on an emergency identifier in signalling and a mapping protocol that turns a caller's location into a PSAP URI. Both can be attacked.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists attacker goals and the attacks that follow, numbered A1 to A8, then derives security requirements R1 to R9 for the mapping protocol and for handling of emergency-marked calls.
tldr.outcome: It gives designers of the mapping protocol a checklist of integrity, authentication, confidentiality and anti-flooding requirements. It is informational.

today: RFC 5069 is an Informational RFC from January 2008, and no other RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. Its terms come from RFC 5012.

sections.title: Marking, Mapping and Scope
sections.content:
Legacy phone users reach emergency services with a well-known number (911 in North America, 112 in Europe), and the system routes the call to the right Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) by caller location. For IP-based calling, two core components are an emergency service identifier, which marks the signalling as an emergency call, and a mapping protocol, which translates that identifier plus the caller's location into a PSAP URL.

Marking lets entities on the signalling path give such messages priority treatment, special processing or special routing. In mapping, a mapping client sends location to a mapping server and receives back a URI used to direct signalling to a PSAP. Routing to the wrong PSAP wastes time while the call taker forwards the call.

The memo restricts itself to attacks on marking and on mapping. Verifying that a reported incident is truthful, and other attacks on PSAP infrastructure using faked location, are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Dialing for help is like asking a map which fire station is closest to you. The call needs a special flag saying it is an emergency, and the map must give the right answer.

sections.title: What Attackers Want
sections.content:
Attacks against the emergency response system have three possible objectives:

  • deny service to all users in an area, from vandalism to terrorism, including a victim who hopes to get faster service by blocking others' calls;
  • gain fraudulent use of services by using the emergency identifier to bypass normal authentication, authorization and accounting;
  • divert emergency calls to non-emergency sites, which can confuse the caller who expects a PSAP operator.

Attacks against an individual either prevent that person from receiving aid, or gather information about an emergency, for example the caller's location, embarrassing facts, or a chance to profit such as a reporter or lawyer seeking business.
sections.eli5: Some tricksters want to jam the phones for everyone, some want free calls, and some want to snoop on one person who asked for help.

sections.title: Attacks on Marking and Mapping
sections.content:
The main attack on marking is fraud. If the attacker is the caller, the routing system trusts the caller's device to supply the right PSAP URI, a provider accepts the call without normal authentication because it carries the emergency identifier, and it routes by the called address without checking that it is a PSAP, then the attacker can reprogram the device to add the identifier to ordinary calls and bypass authorization. The same trick can be used to flood or probe components that handle only emergency calls.

Attacks on mapping fall into three basic kinds: denial of service (flooding the server, taking over the server, or taking over a node the queries pass through), impersonation of the mapping server, and corruption of the mapping database. Attackers may also modify or replay messages. Mapping can also be used against others, for example by tricking the server into sending responses to a victim through a spoofed source address.

To keep one person from getting help, an attacker may prefer to target the mapping client, especially when it is the caller's device. To gain information, an attacker who intercepts mapping traffic can see the location, a PSAP URI, the emergency service identifier (which may reveal fire, police or ambulance) and the addresses of client and server.
sections.eli5: A trickster can stick the emergency flag on a normal call to skip the line, send people to the wrong place, or listen in to learn where someone needs help.

sections.title: The Security Requirements
sections.content:
Section 6 pairs each attack with requirements. Unless stated otherwise, the RFC 2119 words apply to the design of the mapping protocol, not its implementation.

  • R1: for calls meeting conditions a to c, the provider's call routing entity MUST verify that the destination is a PSAP.
  • R2: the mapping protocol MUST NOT create new opportunities for flooding, including amplification.
  • R3: the client MUST be able to verify that a response answers the query it sent.
  • R4 and R5: requests and responses MUST have integrity protection, and the client MUST be able to authenticate the source of responses.
  • R6 and R7: security considerations for server discovery MUST address impersonation, and those for the protocol MUST address database corruption.
  • R8: responses SHOULD include information that lets them be correlated with server logs, to debug misdirected calls.
  • R9: the protocol and its system MUST keep requests and responses confidential.

Probing with the emergency identifier (A2) leads to no new requirement beyond ordinary defences such as firewalls and authentication where possible. Attacks aimed at a specific individual produce no new requirements.
sections.eli5: The rules say: check that an emergency call really goes to an emergency center, make sure answers match questions, keep them from being changed or read by strangers, and do not let the system be used to flood others.

items.label: Fraudulent calls
items.desc: Verify the destination is a PSAP.

items.label: Flooding
items.desc: No new flooding or amplification opportunities.

items.label: Interfering messages
items.desc: Client verifies the response matches its query.

items.label: Database corruption
items.desc: Address corruption and allow log correlation.
